answer.evidence: The arch is two curved tusks, each a 10-14 px wide vertical band that tapers up to a joint at the apex (rows 4-9). The tusks show only their front face, with light and dark shading along the length. There is no horizontal top surface, no front-edge line with eave shadow, and no ellipse. The width profile changes only slightly (10-12 px) down the shafts, so no cap or top plate appears. The snow mounds at the bases (rows 39-45, width 28) are lumpy white heaps of the kind in (d), but they are small base details rather than the main body. The main structure, the arch, is drawn as a flat front elevation with no visible top slope or lintel surface.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin, sparse prop (a curved bone arch with two snow mounds and hanging chains), while the references are whole houses with roofs, walls and doors. By the measured facts it is not shallow: 18 visible tones per tile against 10-12 for the references, 0% near-flat coverage, and only 4% neutral dark edge pixels. That last figure matches the warm brown outline I see beside the bone. By eye, though, the tusk body is a narrow band with about 4 lightness steps (highlight, light, mid, dark), against roughly 6 on the reference roof tiles. It has no per-segment grain or tile-like detail, and the snow bases are two or three tones of white-blue with little form. The chains and sparkles are only a few pixels. Placed beside the richly textured houses it reads thinner and flatter, closer to a clean sticker. The tone count for such a small piece is likely inflated by the few tiles it fills. When in doubt, fail.
